speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: It helped to enable, among other objectives, public agencies to share data safely and purposefully, so that we can serve Singaporeans better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The vision was simple but powerful: a whole-of-Government approach, where agencies can work together using data responsibly, instead of asking citizens to provide the same information repeatedly or navigate multiple agencies on their own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Many Members in this House today were present back when the PSGA Bill was discussed in 2018.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: With your support, today, we have more integrated delivery of public services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Data sharing was also critical during national crises such as COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: At the same time, the PSGA was never only about enabling data sharing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: When the PSGA was debated here in 2018, Members asked for clear rules on data use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: There are clear permitted purposes, controlled access on a need-to-know basis, additional protection for sensitive data and serious consequences for misuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: We have used the PSGA for eight years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: When the PSGA Bill was debated in Parliament in 2018, some Members of Parliament (MPs) saw the potential for PSGA to do more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: They asked about data sharing with trusted partners, like our social service agencies (SSAs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Back then, we had promised to review this later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: And now, we are ready for the next step.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Over time, our public agencies have increasingly partnered trusted organisations outside of the public sector to deliver programmes and reach Singaporeans effectively – especially vulnerable groups where last-mile engagement matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: These include SSAs, community partners and our self-help groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: They have deep networks, cultural understanding and operational presence on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: When we work together with them, support can be more targeted, timely and coordinated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: For example, the Ministry of Education (MOE) works with self-help groups, like the Chinese Development Assistance Council, MENDAKI, SINDA and the Eurasian Association.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: With access to appropriate student data, they can identify and provide targeted support to specific students in their respective ethnic communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The data will also help these partners to assess and improve their programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Similarly, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) works with SG Enable and SSAs to provide an integrated ecosystem of support for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: But for our partnerships to work well, they need relevant data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Today, public agencies rely on individual consent, common law public interest grounds, or sector-specific legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: These avenues are not ideal in many real-world situations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: First, external partners cannot identify who to help if we cannot share that information with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Getting consent means we must first find the people who need help and then ask them for permission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This does not work when external partners should be the first point of contact for hard-to-reach groups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Second, contact details may be outdated and vulnerable individuals may not respond in time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Third, in urgent or large-scale situations, we cannot afford delays caused by seeking consent case-by-case.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: And lastly, when multiple datasets and partners are involved in coordinated support, the consent route becomes onerous and fragmented.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: In all of these situations, relying on consent means that people in need may fall through the cracks and fail to receive timely support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Common law public interest grounds can also be difficult to apply consistently because boundaries are not clearly set out and each case needs extensive assessment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Take MSF's partnership with SG Enable and SSAs in supporting persons with disabilities as an example.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: In order for SG Enable and SSAs to support persons with disabilities in areas like employment assistance, training opportunities and referrals to relevant services, they need the relevant data on persons with disabilities from MSF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: But MSF found it challenging to establish the legal basis for sharing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: So, they went through many rounds of discussions with multiple teams to see if common law public interest applied.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: To reduce legal uncertainty, these SSAs could only get the addresses of persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: They received no other information about disability conditions, needs or demographics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Without this other information, our partners end up spending extra time and effort re-establishing details during visits to our persons with disabilities and their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Members in this House may have heard of these realities on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Families in need end up having to repeat their stories and details to many parties who are actually trying to support them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: It provides a clear legal basis with guardrails for data sharing with our trusted external partners, where it serves legitimate public purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: It does not override other written law, legal privilege or existing contractual restrictions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: It does not authorise data sharing for commercial exploitation, marketing or unrelated purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: And it does not remove the option for public agencies to rely on consent or other legal avenues where these remain appropriate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: First, the Bill retains the existing discipline of the PSGA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Clause 3 ensures there is a legitimate purpose for sharing data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Public agencies can only share data for the same public purposes that govern inter-agency sharing today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: If a use case does not serve these public objectives, public agencies cannot share the data with external partners under the PSGA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: So, for the MSF example I mentioned earlier, the relevant purpose under the PSGA would be well aligned with MSF's mandate to provide support for persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The shared data would help disability SSAs to provide more efficient and targeted support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Second, each data sharing arrangement with an external partner needs specific authorisation by a Minister or his or her delegate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This is the second safeguard under clause 3.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The authorisation must clearly specify what data can be shared, which partner receives it and for what purpose it may be used.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This ensures high-level oversight for each and every arrangement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The public agency must assess the partner's ability to fulfil its role and handle data responsibly with proper security protections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Where the partner is unable to meet the required safeguards, the sharing will not proceed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The third safeguard is ensuring that all external partners are bound by clear Terms of Use that set out how the data is protected and used.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: I spoke earlier about the Government's existing internal rules for data protection and security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Currently, public agencies already need to make sure external partners whom they share data with are able to meet these requirements, and are contractually bound to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: While public agencies already hold external partners to such requirements, we will provide more specific guidance to ensure consistency across different partnerships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: These will include data protection and security requirements, and they will be calibrated to risk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: In other words, this will not be a one-size-fits-all approach.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The more sensitive or confidential the data, the higher the safeguards required.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This will include tighter access controls and stronger encryption and logging.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This ensures that all external partners understand and uphold their responsibility to protect the data and are contractually bound to maintain the necessary safeguards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Today, the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) already criminalises individuals' misuse of personal data held by private organisations or public agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The PDPA sets out offences for the unauthorised use and disclosure of personal data, and unauthorised re-identification of anonymised information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Clause 8 of this Bill introduces related amendments to the PDPA to ensure that these offences can apply to misuse of shared data by individuals from external partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: For non-personal data, the Bill introduces new offences for the unauthorised use or disclosure of shared data by individuals within the external partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Clauses 6 and 7 of the Bill provide for this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Together, the PDPA and the PSGA will provide for complementary offences for stronger deterrence against abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Beyond criminal offences, the Government also retains strong and practical levers, such as: (a) enforcement of contractual Terms of Use; (b) tightening of requirements if an incident reveals additional safeguards are necessary; and (c) where appropriate, revoking authorisation and ceasing the data sharing arrangement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: As the latter is not explicitly stated today, this amendment will clarify, to avoid any doubt, that public agencies are permitted to use their own data to work more effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This removes unnecessary uncertainty and administrative delay, while maintaining the same discipline.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: For example, in 2023, MOE had planned a new survey called Parents' Voices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This was to understand parents' views on education policies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: MOE already had parents' contact information from student data collected during school admission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This was counterintuitive since MOE could already share such data with other public agencies under PSGA purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: So, this amendment we are making is aligned with the PSGA's original intent to enable the public sector to use data both across and within public agencies to fulfil their functions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: To be clear, this amendment does not apply to external partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Each of our use cases with external partners must be specifically authorised by the relevant Minister.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This is particularly for healthcare delivery purposes across the ecosystem of providers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Where public agencies need NEHR data for healthcare purposes, the HIB governs this use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This applies when a public agency performs a healthcare service, such as medical consultations or laboratory tests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The PSGA will continue to govern data in general, including health information for broader public purposes outside healthcare delivery – for example, de-identified data for policy analysis by other public agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The safeguards that I spoke about earlier will apply to such information shared under PSGA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: MHA conducts job fitness and medical examinations to ensure that individuals are suitable for various deployments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Many of these examinations by MHA will access NEHR data under the HIB because they are statutory medical examinations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: But some job fitness assessments fall outside the HIB's statutory framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: These include fitness assessments for regular uniformed officers to bear arms or take on more demanding deployments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: NEHR information for such assessments would be shared under the PSGA for public safety reasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: MOH will be going through the HIB in greater detail later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: Technology must serve people, and not the other way around.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: We share data because it enables us to serve Singaporeans better.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: And in doing so, we aim to strike the right balance – making data sharing not just more effective, but safer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: This Bill represents a careful evolution of the PSGA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: It extends our data sharing and governance framework that has enabled better services within Government to trusted partnerships beyond Government, all while keeping clear what our purpose is, ensuring that there is high-level oversight, strong safeguards and strong accountability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The enactment of PSGA in 2018 was a watershed moment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: It enabled data across Government to serve citizens under strong governance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: With the proposed amendments, we maintain our commitment to protect data, while addressing the reality that effective service delivery requires trusted partnerships beyond public agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: These amendments will enable vulnerable Singaporeans to receive faster, targeted and more coordinated support, when they need it most.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: The amendments will create clearer legal pathways for responsible partnerships while maintaining rigorous oversight and accountability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: With Members' support to enhance our data sharing regime, this Bill ensures that data serves citizens more effectively and responsibly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Ms Jasmin Lau) (for the Minister of State for Digital Development and Information)
text: And by working closely with our trusted partners for more responsive and integrated service delivery, we can further improve citizens' lives and uplift those who need help.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Much of that debate centred on how to strike the right balance between central oversight and the operational autonomy of Statutory Boards; how to enable effective whole-of-Government coordination; how to provide a clear legal basis for data sharing across agencies; and how to apply governance standards consistently across public bodies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Members also raised deeper questions that remain relevant today: where accountability sits in an increasingly digital state; how we build a data-driven, yet citizen-centric public service; how we break down agency silos; and how governance frameworks can enable, rather than constrain, our Smart Nation ambitions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At its core, the 2018 debate was about governance and boundaries: managing risk, clarifying authority and ensuring accountability as the public sector transformed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Eight years on, we can see clearly how the PSGA has enabled many of the milestones set out in the Digital Government Blueprint.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Whole-of-Government services, integrated digital platforms and the "once-only" principle are no longer abstract policy aspirations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These are not just efficiency gains; they translate directly into people receiving help more quickly and with less friction.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For those of us who regularly assist residents with appeals, we also see both how far we have come and where more can still be done.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Even today, we sometimes wish for deeper integration, so that residents in need do not have to navigate multiple applications or repeatedly submit the same information.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And we can no longer imagine a Public Service where backend systems are fragmented, because we know the administrative inefficiencies this would create and, more importantly, how easily people could fall through the cracks simply because the system was too complex or too burdensome to access.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singaporeans intuitively understand the value of data sharing when it is used to meet real public needs, whether to deliver services more smoothly or to reduce administrative burden on businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But as we scale these capabilities, the central issue before us today is no longer just governance efficiency or administrative accountability.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Trust that data is used responsibly and only for its intended purpose.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Trust that it is protected, not misused or manipulated to the disadvantage of individuals or businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And critically, trust that can be sustained as data sharing extends beyond direct Government agencies to external partners and ecosystems; introducing, inevitably, more points of vulnerability that must be carefully managed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This debate marks an important evolution: from managing boundaries within Government, to how we build, safeguard and scale trust in a digital state that increasingly operates beyond its traditional reach.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As we do so, it is essential that we scale securely, protect the data of Singaporeans and hold external partners to the same high standards that Singaporeans rightly expect of the Government.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is against this backdrop that the MDDI GPC and fellow People's Action Party (PAP) MPs seek clarifications across several key themes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These clarifications are not raised to slow progress, but to ensure that as we extend data sharing beyond direct government control and unlock further benefits for our people and businesses, we continue to uphold the trust that underpins public confidence in our digital systems.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Allow me to briefly outline these themes before elaborating on my own.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: GPC and PAP MPs Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Henry Kwek will elaborate on this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Bill is being debated ahead of the HIB, which focuses on safeguarding health data for healthcare delivery.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The interaction between these two Bills raises important questions on scope, safeguards, accountability and how the amended PSGA interfaces with other legislation governing data use.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My fellow GPC Member Ms Choo Pei Ling will address this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What capabilities must partners possess before data is entrusted to them and how do we ensure compliance is robust, yet not overly onerous?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In our deliberations, the GPC recognises that there are many types of data; ranging from anonymised and aggregated data, to business and economic, and sensitive data relating to personal data and critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How do we adopt a tiered, risk-based approach that balances control with efficiency?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Henry Kwek, Ms Jessica Tan and I will speak further on this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the core of this Bill is the objective of delivering public goods better and doing so safely.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There could also be a group of partners who have demonstrated a strong track record of delivering positive public outcomes but may need assistance in strengthening their data infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The GPC will propose supporting such external partners to mature their digital system so that they can continue to serve residents better.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Who approves data sharing arrangements and what safeguards are in place?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When data is shared with external partners, how do we ensure transparency on what is shared and the processes it goes through?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng will share views on this, including proposing possible oversight mechanisms such as reporting or periodic reviews.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Fifth, ongoing cybersecurity assurance once data exchange is operational and protection against cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou and I will touch on this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As the cybersecurity community often reminds us, it is not a question of if a breach occurs, but when.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How are external partners held accountable should a breach occur on their end, particularly in the context of PSGA and PDPA?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Henry Kwek will address this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In this regard, the MDDI Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC), together with the People's Action Party (PAP) Members of Parliament, seek several important clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These clarifications are not intended to slow progress, but to ensure that when data sharing is extended beyond direct Government control, we continue to uphold public trust in our digital systems, while further enhancing its benefits to citizens and businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The core of this discussion is not merely about data or systems, but about people's lives.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is about how data is used to facilitate transactions for Singaporeans, expedite assistance to those in need and ensure no one is left behind – while at the same time, allowing us to safeguard the security, privacy and trust that citizens have placed upon us.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, allow me to elaborate on my own clarifications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: First, on assessing the readiness and capability of external partners entrusted with public data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Within Government, agencies are required to meet established standards such as Instruction Manual 8 (IM8) compliance, secure hosting environments, robust incident-response capabilities and many others and these are regularly audited.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In particular, I seek clarification on the standards that will be imposed; the audit rights Government will retain and the intended audit regime or frequency; whether partners will be assessed through self-declaration, pre-project assessments, or ongoing assurance; on how risks arising from subcontractors engaged by these partners will be managed; and how liability and breach accountability will be clearly structured in contractual terms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Which brings me to my second point: data classification and proportionality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Information technology (IT) practitioners will recognise that the safest way to manage risk in this scenario is, in theory, not to allow data sharing at all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But the clear benefits of responsible data sharing; seen in schemes such as GSTV, Workfare and employment credits, and all the examples cited by Minister of State Jasmin Lau earlier, show that this is not a tenable position today.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Avoiding risk entirely comes at a real cost to citizens.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our residents have asked for greater integration across Government services, and our lived experience in assisting with appeals shows both how far we have come and how much more we can still do to make lives better for our people and businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That said, not all data carries the same level of risk.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some data may be aggregated or anonymised; some may involve businesses or economic information; and other data may involve personal information or touch on critical infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A risk-based, tiered approach; matching partner requirements to the nature of the data, could reduce unnecessary burden on partners while maintaining strong safeguards, and allow our data sharing ecosystem to remain nimble and responsive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the same time, while standards, audits and controls are necessary when data is shared with external partners, they must be implemented in a way that is administratively efficient and not overly onerous, while still meeting the intent of safeguarding data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And most importantly, this framework must be operationally resourced.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Assurance cannot rest solely on self-declaration, especially when dealing with sensitive data.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It must be supported by credible, enforceable oversight that keeps pace with the scale and the sensitivity of data sharing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Third, on partners that deliver strong public outcomes but may lack the digital maturity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We must not lose sight that the ultimate objective of this Bill is to deliver strong public outcomes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Their digital limitations should not diminish their ability to deliver public good, nor risk unintentionally excluding those who need help most.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we agree that it is important that data is available, where needed, to ensure that public services are allowed to reach as wide an audience as possible and to enable agencies to get assistance to vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, data empowers policy-making that is more responsive to the needs of a diverse population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, we do agree that data must be accessible to entities and partners in order to achieve this, and that data be used to enable better delivery of public services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, the question before us today is not simply whether data should be shared or used.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also about how power over the sharing and use of data is governed and what guardrails are in place where such power is exercised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also would benefit from having express channels of recourse known and accessible widely that would come into play, if and when mistakes occur from misuse or abuse of data.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such a shift from a more rule-based model of data governance to one that relies more heavily on executive decision and ultimately, discretion, should be founded in necessity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we do not automatically disagree with this shift in principle, the public should understand why this change is being proposed and why now.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And from these examples, can the Minister articulate the common characteristics that would indicate when Ministerial discretion was warranted?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And will these characterisations be codified as guidance for future authorisations?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Had the agencies previously attempted other approaches, such as, for example, for persons with disabilities and their families attempting to gain consent upfront from affected individuals to share the full suite of data to community partners, which are not public agencies, in order to better provide services?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I said earlier, allowing sharing to be made subject to a Minister's discretion is not automatically wrong.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a complex system with many moving parts, it is probably often necessary.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But as with all our governance institutions, executive discretion has to be bounded, reviewable and transparent, especially when it concerns citizens' data.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is even more so when that data is highly sensitive.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I need not remind everyone that data is king, given that we live in a world of scams, impersonation, data theft and identity theft, now enhanced by generative and exponentially improving artificial intelligence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is provided for in the Bill that directions must not be inconsistent with written law or to impede independently statutory functions, it is not clear to me how these limits will operate in practice under the expanded scope proposed by the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not about ascribing nefarious intentions to current officeholders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is about the institutional design and guardrails that need to be built around such powers to be granted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What recourse exists if a decision is later found to be erroneous or disproportionate?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also foreseeable that the proposed amendments could have implications beyond personal data.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Any number of businesses now exist that attempt to commercialise personal data that is collected before attempting to monetise these data, whether through outright sale of such datasets, targeted advertising or using it to craft more commercially competitive strategies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, public or agencies also often hold commercially sensitive information, proprietary business data or intellectual property belonging to firms that engage with the public sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not inconceivable that personal data, especially when aggregated is, by its nature, valuable, especially when dealing in instances, such as the people sector.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Bill criminalises unauthorised disclosure or misuse of disclosed data by employees of external parties, this does not fully address the risk of legitimate but unintended commercial or anti-competitive effects.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could take the form of an external contractor gaining access to sensitive data about a competitor when data is shared legitimately under a broad authorisation to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would there be clear expectations to exclude, anonymise or otherwise protect such information by default?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister also clarify when issuing a data sharing direction, what specific factors must be evaluated?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, Saudi Arabia recently issued rules for secondary use of data, which establishes a framework for sharing data beyond its original collection for public interest, research and innovation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Those rules explicitly state, for instance, that the data sharing entity reserves the right to incorporate provisions concerning intellectual property rights and commercial confidentiality within the usage licence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Bill emphasises that PDPA obligations continue to apply and that criminal penalties extend to non-public sector recipients, citizens may wonder what are the explicit safeguards or channels of recourse they have to protect their privacy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially in the instance where the data is highly sensitive, such as personal or family medical records.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Redress should not only be about fines or punishment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clear, accessible pathways for recourse are essential to maintaining public trust as data flows become more complex.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Once sensitive personal data is leaked, it could potentially compromise a person's financial situation, access to key services and those of their family as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It could affect the financial, commercial and competitive position of a firm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Should serious data breaches occur and recourse be difficult, that could undermine that very public trust that the Bill rests upon and which the Singapore system has painstakingly built up over decades.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could take the form of including data sharing, breaches, remedies and vulnerabilities, and efforts to strengthen procedures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also have clearer rules and principles that must be applied when Ministerial directions are made for the sharing of data with information about the avenues available to the public to seek redress should their sensitive personal data be misused or even leaked.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we improve our data systems to better communicate and implement policies to better serve Singaporeans, let us ensure that we continue to have measures in place to protect and safeguard sensitive data in order for them to have trust in the institutions that are ultimately meant to be there to serve and support them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Since its introduction in 2018, the PSGA has strengthened the way Government agencies work together, especially in how they share and use data.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This makes a real and meaningful difference to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When agencies can exchange information safely and responsibly, families in need can receive help more quickly, agencies can plan interventions and reduce duplications, eligibility checks for support schemes do not require applications, for example, the GSTV, healthcare subsidies and the Silver Support Scheme, and businesses experience smoother, more coordinated support.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Act also makes clear that data is shared only for genuine public interest purposes and always with strong safeguards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Public Sector Governance (Amendment) Bill we are debating today seeks to update PSGA so that the Government agencies can share data with trusted external partners, with the right safeguards in place.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will help deliver services to the public more effectively and seamlessly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as we discuss the Public Sector Governance (Amendment) Bill, I want to focus on a set of practical questions that matter to Singaporeans: how will the Government agency decide when data can be shared with external partners?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And how do we ensure that every external partner entrusted with public sector data is truly capable of protecting it?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These questions are at the core of public trust.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans expect that when their information is shared across agencies or with external partners who help deliver public services, that it is done with care, transparently and only when it genuinely serves the public interest.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how will the Government agency decide when data can be shared with external partners?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What this means is that data cannot be shared just because it is convenient or efficient for agencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It must clearly support a real public need – whether that is helping residents receive services more smoothly, ensuring essential functions continue during disruptions or strengthening the stewardship of public funds, or enabling agencies to work together to solve complex problems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: At its heart, the principle is simple: data should only be shared when it genuinely benefits people, is appropriate for the situation and is backed by a strong public interest reason.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We also need strong documentation because every decision to share data ultimately affects real people.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If the partner is outside the public sector, an additional layer of authorisation is required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This two-tier structure ensures that agencies spell out clearly why the data is needed, what exactly will be shared, what safeguards must be in place and who is accountable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is important and I am glad that the Bill specifies this because it creates a transparent audit trail that shows not just what is to be shared but why, with whom and under what conditions?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Most importantly, it ensures that these decisions are not made quietly or casually at an operational level.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are reviewed and approved at the right level of leadership, with clear responsibility for protecting the trust Singaporeans have placed with the Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The public sector operates under stricter rules for managing government data while external partners are governed by the PDPA.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This ensures that anyone who is entrusted with public data is held to the same legal standard of responsibility and protection.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I must stress that penalties alone do not remove risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need assurance that partners have the right systems, training and safeguards in place before any data is shared.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As more public services are delivered through digital platforms, vendor systems and community partners, one thing has become very clear – data protection cannot rely on the good intentions of individuals alone.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Most incidents do not just happen because someone acted maliciously.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They can happen because a system was not designed well, a process was unclear or an organisation did not invest in the right safeguards.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In other words, the risks today are increasingly systemic, not just personal.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the question for every agency that intends to share data is – how is an external partner assessed beyond just checking for compliance on paper?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It means understanding their partners' technical safeguards, their governance structure, their staff training, their incident response processes and their ability to meet the conditions set out in the Ministerial direction.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It means ensuring that they can protect data not just in theory, but in practice, day to day, across their systems and across their teams.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ultimately, this is about protecting the trust that Singaporeans place in our public institutions.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is not about duplicating the PDPA, which already governs private sector data practice.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What matters is that every partner can show that their system works in practice, not just on paper.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I want to stress again that the intent is not to add burden to our partners because we want their services to be delivered.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we have to find that balance of how to ensure that this is done securely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With all these measures, I think we can also recognise that it is not going to take risk away completely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What it is, is to look at how we can minimise or prevent data breaches.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To make this real, public agencies and partners must treat data as a shared, ongoing responsibility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This means building a culture where leaders set clear expectations, staff are trained and supported, and systems are regularly tested and improved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It means learning from incidents, not hiding them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It means working closely with partners to close gaps early rather than waiting for problems to surface.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But I would like to place some significant concerns on the record.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This contradicted earlier assurances that the data was "purely for contact tracing, period".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The then-Minister in-charge of the Smart Nation acknowledged he had been blindsided.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: He had not considered existing laws when making those assurances.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The backlash was significant not because Singaporeans opposed law enforcement but because they felt misled about how their data would be used.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The lesson is that trust must be built through demonstrably robust processes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once faith in a data sharing framework is broken, it is expensive to rebuild.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I raise this because the Bill before us creates a new framework for sharing citizen data, this time, with private entities.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The question is whether we have learnt from the TraceTogether episode.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The original PSGA passed in 2018 allowed Government agencies to share data with one another under Ministerial direction.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When MSF shares client data with family service centres and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), we see coordinated assistance and faster assessments.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Government gains the capability to share any data with any private entity.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Private entities gain access to Government health data.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Citizens did not know Police could access their data.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Why risk the same failure mode again with this Bill on a larger scale, with more actors, including those outside the Government, and less visibility?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If this Bill expands what the Government can do with citizen data, should it not also expand what citizens can do to track, to benefit from and to govern that sharing?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: All data sharing directions issued to private entities should be published – the categories of data shared, the recipient, the purpose, the duration.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is the disclosure of Ministerial directions made in small numbers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Australia's Data Availability and Transparency Act 2022 includes such a register.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: TraceTogether's problem was that citizens could not know how their data was used – and a register solves this.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, question one: would the Government commit to publishing a register of all data sharing directions issued to private entities?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When data flows from the Government to the private sector, it creates value for those two players.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Private entities gain data access and improve their services.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What is the mechanism ensuring citizens share in that value?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I mean concrete improvements: service quality guarantees, cost reductions passed to users, transparency about outcomes and also something I believe in, which is benefit sharing from any future possible monetisation of their data.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, question two: what benefits will Singaporean citizens see from this framework?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And will there be any part of the Government that advocates directly for citizens gaining a share of these data benefits?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The original PSGA allowed sharing between Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This amendment opens the door to the private sector powers of a different order.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Australia's framework includes a review that "must start by and be completed within 12 months or a longer period agreed by the Minister of the third anniversary of the commencement of this Act".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The grant of novel powers should have built-in moments for reassessment.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The backlash to TraceTogether led to emergency legislation limiting Police access.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The public consultation promised robust safeguards through data governance requirements on external partners – I quote, "requirements similar to what public sector agencies have to meet".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Individual criminal liability for employees who misuse data.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: No security certification, no audit trails, no breach notification duties.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, question four: where are the data governance requirements promised in the consultation?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And if they are to come by regulation or procurement contract terms, will the Ministry commit to that today?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Under PDPA, for data breaches involving personal data, organisations face financial penalties of up to 10% of their annual turnover.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Under this Bill, for non-personal data shared with private entities, only individual employees can be prosecuted.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If an organisation systematically exploits non-personal Government data beyond its authorised purpose, the entity that designed the business model and profited, faces no direct liability.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If organisations can profit from misuse while only individuals bear risk, the incentive structure is incorrect.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, question five: will the Government commit to organisational accountability mechanisms, especially for non-personal data which is not covered by PDPA?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And why has it not chosen to hold organisations accountable here?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In any case, deeper public-private collaboration is inevitable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I trust that the points collectively raised today will spare us a future blindsiding.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The PSGA establishes the overarching framework for data governance across public agencies, including provisions for sharing health data beyond clinical care – for policy planning, service delivery and community outreach.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In contrast, the HIB is designed to safeguard health data primarily for healthcare delivery.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The intersection of these two regimes raises important questions about scope, safeguards and accountability.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The foremost concern among Singaporeans is the extent to which sensitive health data will be shared under the PSGA and whether safeguards are sufficiently robust to prevent misuse.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents want assurance that their most personal information – medical histories, disabilities, mental health records – will not be casually accessed or repurposed.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance MSF may share health risk indicators and demographic data with SG Enable and SSAs to proactively reach out to people with disabilities for job-matching and to our seniors for caregiver support.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such proactive outreach is commendable – it improves lives, strengthens preventive care and ensures that vulnerable groups are not left behind.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, these examples also underscore the sensitivity of health data being used for social policy, community outreach and service coordination.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The line between beneficial use and overreach must be carefully guarded.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The general concern is execution – how usage and safeguards are implemented on the ground.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are agencies sufficiently resourced with trained personnel, secure infrastructure and modern cybersecurity tools to enforce these safeguards?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We seek the Government’s assurance that appropriate funding and resources are allocated for talent, hardware and software.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These requirements cannot be waived without consulting MOH.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It would undermine public trust if agencies could bypass this by requesting the same information under PSGA.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To further enhance trust, I propose that the Government jointly maintain a public register of all use cases where health data has been shared under PSGA for non-health purposes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The register should specify the authorising Minister, the external partner, the general purpose and the categories of data shared, without disclosing sensitive operational details.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such a register, updated regularly, would reassure Singaporeans that health data sharing beyond healthcare delivery is tightly controlled, exceptional and subject to public oversight.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On future-proofing safeguards, could Singapore explore privacy-preserving technologies, such as anonymisation, differential privacy or federated learning, to enable data-driven insights without exposing raw health records?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These technologies are increasingly adopted worldwide to balance innovation with privacy.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The PSGA amendments empower the Government to partner effectively with community organisations for public benefit.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With robust safeguards – Ministerial authorisation, cybersecurity requirements, criminal penalties and mandatory consent for sensitive uses – health data can, indeed, be shared responsibly where genuine public interest exists.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But transparency, accountability and public trust must remain at the heart of this framework.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At its core, this Bill strengthens the Government’s ability to deliver help that is effective, timely and dignified.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In practice, the Government does not serve Singaporeans alone.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It works with social service agencies and community partners to deliver care with empathy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It also works with the private sector to deliver services efficiently and at scale.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And to do this well, it often needs to pull together the right facts from different sources, so that those who need help most can receive the right support quickly and in a coordinated way.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Information does not always flow smoothly sometimes across agencies and often between Government and trusted partners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of us in Parliament see the consequences when we help our residents in their appeals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some residents must submit the same documents multiple times.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some must recount painful parts of their story more than once before support can be put together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Not everybody can navigate the system with ease.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And some do fall through the cracks, not because officers or partners do not care, but because the right information needs time to gather for the right persons to act.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And that is why I support this Bill and its direction.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is a practical step forward from the status quo and it aims to strike a better balance between service delivery, privacy and security.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And it recognises a simple truth – data sharing must not be driven by convenience.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It must be controlled, accountable and safe, especially when we share data with external partners.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because this Bill will has wide impact, I have three questions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Examples that show better support for those who need social and financial assistance, better coordination across services and stronger outreach, especially for seniors, preventive care and active ageing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some examples may be immediate, others longer-term, but it will help us understand and have a clearer sense of the early priorities and aspirations and how the Government fully intends to tap this Bill to better our people’s lives.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second, the Government works with many partners of different sizes and capabilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And where strategic partners need this information to serve residents well but lack capability, how will the Government help level them up?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, I call for the Government to provide common frameworks, grants, training, shared platforms and secure ways for partners to plug in, so that all partners, even the smaller ones, can meet the requirements without being overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singaporeans expect data to be safeguarded well and we also expect strong consequences for misuse.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, threats are becoming more sophisticated and even well-run organisations can be targeted by persistent attacks or malware.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While we must keep the bar high and always learn from past mistakes, we must also avoid swinging to the other extreme, setting requirements or consequences so onerous that capable partners hesitate to work with the Government.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must also guard against the Public Service getting excessively risk averse that they do not even want to share even with this expanded framework and therefore, lose the chance to serve our people better.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For example, what is the baseline standard for all partners and what higher standards must apply for more sensitive data and what support will be given to help partners meet these standards?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And the next point, and an important point, if a serious incident happens despite reasonable safeguards by these partners, given how widespread cybersecurity breaches are globally, how will the Government assess responsibility in a way that is fair, firm and predictable so that our partners have clarity and confidence to work with us?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope the Government will take this chance to engage partners closely as implementation begins, so that the safeguards are not just strong on paper but also workable in practice.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the appropriate safeguards to prevent misuse, this amendment Bill will enable targeted and effective delivery of social services to those who need it the most.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My Toa Payoh Central residents, with a significant elderly population, is supported by various social service providers, such as Care Corner, TOUCH, Dementia Singapore, NTUC Health, People’s Association, as well as many other local community healthcare services and organisations.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Non-public social service providers would benefit from greater collaboration and information-sharing with the public sector agencies serving the same community needs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similar to how schemes like the Housing and Development Board Flat Eligibility process and ComCare financial assistance require pulling of data from various sources, I agree that the enhancements will allow for timely access in delivering support and ensuring that no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In order to better enable the delivery of social services to our communities, I have two points of clarifications for the Minister’s consideration.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We live in a day and age where no organisation is safe from cyberattacks, including our social service providers and charitable organisations.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, in May 2019, more than 4,000 individuals had their personal information leaked after part of the reputable blood donation organisation’s website was hacked.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Personal names, contact numbers, email addresses, declared blood types, preferred appointment dates and times and preferred locations for blood donations were compromised.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: According to the Singapore Cybersecurity Health Report in 2023, which surveyed more than 2,000 small, medium and large organisations in Singapore, over eight in 10 organisations encountered a cybersecurity incident that year.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whether in the form of encryption standards or increased incident response capabilities, how regularly would these safeguards be reviewed?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Risk profiles and ownership may change over time as organisations change systems, employees or subcontractors.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Regular audits and reviews of the cybersecurity capabilities of external partners would ensure a safe and secure transfer of data between the public and non-public sectors.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I am sure what many SSAs will also want to know is the details of the terms of funding, which will be allocated specifically for beefing up of their IT infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Individual accountability is important, especially in cases where a single individual or a small group of individuals may be directly responsible for the misuse of shared data.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, in other data incidents, responsibility is unable to be traced back to one single employee.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The failure may be organisational, for example, due to weak internal controls, poor access governance or inadequate training.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In those cases, it is especially important for a strong framework of organisational liability to exist, to ensure that liability can be correctly attributed to a wider variety of situations.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, under the PDPA, the Personal Data Protection Commission can impose financial penalties against an organisation for intentional or negligent contraventions of PDPA.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This may be necessary considering the sensitivity of the information shared by the Government with non-public entities.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These additional measures will ensure that the public continues entrusting personal data to the Government and, by extension, its external partners, upholding its commitment to data security.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I support this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I want to speak of data as eyesight, the visibility that allows the Government to see what is happening in people's lives, especially at the margins.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When the Government holds data but cannot share it effectively with trusted partners on the ground, it becomes partially blind.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When the system cannot see clearly, it is not policy that fails first.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is people, especially the vulnerable, who fall through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill seeks to address that blind spot by enabling responsible data sharing beyond the public sector.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I support this move, it raises fundamental questions about agency, accountability, safeguards, transparency and trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even after sharing, the public agency remains the controller under PDPA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Legal control does not always translate into felt control.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I acknowledge that consent is often not practicable, especially when data is needed urgently to identify those in need.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
