text: However, urgency is not a licence for opacity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While agencies may not know every future downstream collaborator, the Bill rightly requires them to specify the external partners, purpose and scope.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If an agency does not know who it is sharing with, it should not share at all.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From a resident's perspective, consent is not merely a checkbox.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When consent cannot be the default, what replaces it as a reassurance?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When a resident walks into a Family Service Centre, they experience the system as one whole.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They do not distinguish between a Ministry, a charity or a contractor.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet under this Bill, their data may flow across all these actors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will residents be told clearly, plainly and at the right time, that their information is being shared?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When something goes wrong, will they know whom to turn to first, instead of being bounced between agencies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, not all data sharing is life critical, some are for administrative convenience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such cases, will residents have a practical way to express discomfort?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill provides no opt-out, so reassurance must come from transparency and restraint, not silence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Efficiency matters, but it must never eclipse agency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For many residents, "anonymisation" is understood as a permanent promise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The idea that it can be reversed, even lawfully, feels unsettling.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Used well, it can help agencies identify unmet needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government explain that anonymisation is not an absolute state, but one that may be reversed under tightly authorised circumstances?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister assure us that re-identified data will never be used for predictive scoring affecting access to housing, insurance, loans or employment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ministerial approval is a high bar, but for large cohorts or sensitive data, should there be independent ethical review, similar to health research purposes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Re-identification must exist to help people, to connect dots for protection, never to label or stigmatise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I also note that data should be retained only for as long as needed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Purpose completion should trigger deletion, not secondary utility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why should anonymised datasets continue to be held by external partners once the authorised purpose is complete?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Under the Bill, sharing with non-public sector persons requires Ministerial authorisation, which may be delegated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This use case specific model supports agility, but delegation raises a simple question: where does the buck stop?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Transparency matters because delegation should not dilute responsibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, would it be more robust to have high-risk or large-scale decisions reviewed by a small standing board rather than a single official?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Trust grows when systems can be verified, not merely asserted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we confident the PSGA and PDPA framework leaves no gaps where technical classification determines liability rather than real harm?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I understand external partners will be subject to Terms of Use requiring strict security standards.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A breach at the weakest partner compromises the entire ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Smaller charities acting in good faith must be supported, while large vendors must be held to higher standards befitting their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While data sharing directions are internal instruments, the stated aim is enhanced transparency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will residents receive plain-language explanations of how and why their data is shared?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could MDDI commit to an annual public report summarising data sharing directions and authorisations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this information be accessible to seniors and those with limited English proficiency?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Four-year-old Megan Khung did not die because no one cared.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: She died because the signals that might have protected her never came together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A preschool saw injuries; a social worker identified risks; family members raised concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Each saw a part of the picture, but the system never saw clearly, early enough or as one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: No law can guarantee that such tragedies will never happen again.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But Parliament has a responsibility to ask whether we can build systems that can see better, respond earlier and act together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If data is eyesight, then sharing must help the system see, not blur its vision.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If data is eyesight, then re-identification must protect the vulnerable, not label them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If data is eyesight, then accountability must be visible, not lost in layers of delegation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And if consent cannot always be practicable, then we owe residents something just as important in return: clarity about what is done with their data, dignity in how decisions are made and confidence that responsibility is clearly held.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill gives us tools, but tools alone do not guarantee wisdom.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What matters is how we choose to use them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will govern data so the system can see clearly, so that people can live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is the work before us, not to just to pass this Bill, but to exercise its powers with restraint, care and moral clarity; not just to enable data sharing, but to earn and keep the trust of the people we serve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us ensure that when the system sees, it sees together and when it acts, it acts in time.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Several Members raised questions on the scope and the safeguards for data sharing with external partners.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Expanding PSGA is like building more bridges to help more people cross safely and access support earlier.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Every bridge must be built with a clear public purpose.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Not for curiosity, not for convenience and not for commercial gains, but to connect our people to something essential.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Access to the bridges must also be properly authorised.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Not everyone can direct traffic across the bridge or change its structure.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And likewise, data access will be tightly governed, with clear and defined approval processes, roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: As the usage of these bridges grow, we must ensure that those who operate and maintain the bridges are capable and ready.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This means that we will assess and uplift both the public sector and our trusted partners' capabilities so that they can be trusted custodians of the data that they receive.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Trust is sustained through accountability and transparency – through regular inspections, monitoring and audits.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And when something goes wrong, a responsible system responds decisively.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: We close, we fix, we make the bridge safe again.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: That is why we have clear incident management processes.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: We do not give up on building the bridges altogether.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This is how we help more people while strengthening trust.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Because trust is not meant to be a brake that holds us back.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: I will now address specific points that Members raised.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Henry Kwek asked for concrete examples of how the Bill will improve outcomes – particularly for those around us who need social and financial assistance, especially for our seniors and our children.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: I shared a few examples in my opening speech on how the PSGA framework has enabled more integrated delivery of support within Government.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: With this Bill, we can extend this approach to partnerships with SSAs, community partners and self-help groups – organisations with deep networks, cultural understanding and presence on the ground.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou mentioned many social service providers that support his Toa Payoh Central residents – Care Corner, TOUCH, Dementia Singapore, NTUC Health and others.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: These partners can benefit from data sharing with public agencies, serving the same community needs.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Families in difficulty need not repeat their circumstances to multiple parties.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And the staff working in these social service providers can focus their time and their energies on providing tangible help, rather than collect duplicative information again.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Kwek, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how the public can be assured that their data would be used appropriately.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And central to all of this is our focus on building and safeguarding trust, as noted by Mr Sharael Taha.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Data sharing must serve public purposes as provided for under the PSGA.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: To borrow Ms Tan's words, data is not shared just because it is convenient or efficient for public agencies, but it must clearly support a real public need.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The two main categories where Government will share and use data for remain unchanged.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: That is, data will be used for better delivery of services to the individual and for policy analysis and formulation.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Ms He Ting Ru claimed that we are shifting from a rule-based framework to executive discretion in data sharing.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The existing PSGA stipulates seven purposes under which a Ministerial direction may be made for data sharing these clear purposes, as well as all existing data governance rules remain fully in place.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: These purposes make it clear that citizens must benefit before data can be shared.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: So, Mr Kenneth Tiong may have misunderstood, but there will be no situation where we share data with partners for their commercial benefit.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This authorisation by the Minister is not a replacement for rules, but an additional safeguard.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Before data is shared with external partners, it must go through careful deliberation within the Public Service, culminating in a sign off by the Minister or his or her delegate.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: To Mr Yip's question on the delegation of Minister's authorisation, delegation if done, will only be to the senior leadership level of the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Any delegation will be made public as provided for under the Interpretation Act.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The third safeguard is that our partners must comply with Terms of Use.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Retention periods for the data will be specified and requirements to purge data when the retention period has ended will be mandated.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: External partners will also have to provide yearly declarations of compliance with the Terms of Use.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: On top of these, there will also be higher requirements for more sensitive data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: For instance, periodic audit checks at a higher frequency when more sensitive data is involved.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: These checks will be conducted by the agency or qualified third parties appointed by the agency.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Highly sensitive data will also require reviewing of privileged accounts monthly for access rights.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Before any data sharing is established, such terms, of course, will be discussed with the external partner to ensure that they are able to comply.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: As our trusted external partners may face liability under the contractual terms, both the public agency and the external partner must be confident that the requirements can be complied with.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling and Mr Yip asked about our principles for data protection and sharing.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: As Dr Choo noted, public agencies also use privacy-preserving technologies to limit unnecessary exposure of data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Where personal data is concerned, public agencies must continue to exercise judgement even if the statutory requirements allow for sharing with external partners should this Bill be passed.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: In cases like this where the data use is highly sensitive, an additional impact assessment may be made and consent sought, even though, it is not statutorily required.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This is another example where more safeguards are put in place in proportion to the risk.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: To Mr Yip and Ms He's questions about re-identification of anonymised data, this was already debated in 2018.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: For example, when certain datasets are corrupted or destroyed and re-identification is needed to continue delivering services to citizens.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Several Members also suggested providing a list of external partners authorised under the PSGA.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Today, public agencies work with many partners on diverse purposes, often on an ad hoc basis, and it could be challenging to share, in detail, a list of external partners or notify citizens for every use, given the dynamic nature of these partnerships.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: But we thank Members for the suggestion and we will review this at a later date once we have sufficient experience with the Bill.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Individuals with concerns about how their personal data is being used can approach the relevant public agencies or the external partner.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: They can also report suspected misuse of their personal data or report data incidents through the Government Data Incident Reporting Platform.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Cai and Mr Kwek asked about cybersecurity expectations for our external partners.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And Mr Cai also rightly noted that no organisation is immune to cyberattacks.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: As I shared, our approach is to set standards proportionate to risk.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: We have baseline standards that all partners must meet, with more stringent requirements when sensitive data is involved.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: When the data security space evolves and new requirements are needed, public agencies will also update the Terms of Use so that our external partners are well-positioned to protect data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Kwek and Mr Yip asked about smaller partners who may lack resources.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And Mr Cai similarly asked about how external partners would be expected to maintain safeguards against sophisticated attacks.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: A smaller entity may handle data sets that are as sensitive as larger partners and hence lowering the requirements simply due to them being smaller entities will not be proportional to the level of data risk.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Instead, our public agencies will work with our external partners to build the capabilities where necessary for the proper and responsible management of data shared with them.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This was a point raised by Mr Sharael.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: As Ms Tan had suggested, this may involve ensuring robust systems, strong training and proper controls.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Kwek also suggested for MDDI and the Government Technology Agency of Singapore, to provide common tools or shared platforms to help smaller organisations and partners meet the requirements.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Cai asked whether the Ministry will consider financial penalties against organisations that misuse data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And Mr Cai is right that not all data incidents can be traced to a single employee.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Failures may be organisational in nature, arising from weak internal controls, poor access governance or inadequate training.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: External partners must comply with the obligations under the PDPA, such as maintaining reasonable security requirements preventing unauthorised access.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) can impose financial penalties on organisations for intentional or negligent contraventions.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This also applies to personal data shared under the PSGA framework.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: So, the organisational penalties that Mr Cai asked about are already available under existing law.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: I earlier mentioned many times the Terms of Use that public agencies will impose on external partners.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Organisations receiving Government's data must comply with the data protection and security safeguards in the Terms of Use and may face liability under these contractual terms for breaches.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Yip also asked if the severity of offences is large enough to deter bad actors.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The possibility of imprisonment for misusing data is a significant deterrent.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Kwek and Mr Yip have raised concerns about data incidents.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: All data incidents reported to Government will be properly looked into.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Public agencies will take remedial actions to limit the impact of an incident, investigate and address vulnerabilities, and also to recover equipment and data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The Government will also continue to report on data incidents.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: External partners are obligated to report to the public agency or to PDPC when significant data incidents occur.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Kwek asked how Government will assess responsibility in a way that is firm, fair and predictable, if a serious incident happens despite reasonable safeguards.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Liability is assessed in context: we look at all of the facts and the circumstances, and we consider the nature of the incident, whether reasonable safeguards were in place, and the actions of the parties involved, including their response to the incident.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Partners who act in good faith and made reasonable efforts to implement proper safeguards will be treated fairly.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Those who are reckless or negligent will be held to account.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Tiong raised TraceTogether as a cautionary tale.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: When the issue arose, the Government came to Parliament, explained the position and clarified the legal framework.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: We did not hide from scrutiny, we addressed it openly in this House.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Second, TraceTogether did not undermine public trust in the way Mr Tiong suggests.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: They understood the Government's explanation and the safeguards that were put in place.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: To characterise it as a fiasco that broke public trust is not borne out by how Singaporeans actually responded.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The lesson from TraceTogether is not that Government cannot be trusted with data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: It is that when questions arise, the Government must be accountable and transparent – and we were.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Mr Yip asked whether citizens can be permitted to opt out of data sharing with our external partners.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The data sharing serves broad public sector policy, planning and service delivery objectives.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Allowing individuals to opt out would lead to incomplete data, which will fundamentally undermine our ability to plan, formulate policies and deliver services.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Take planning for social services as an example.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: If individuals opt out, the data that public agencies and external partners have will be incomplete.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This could mean under-provisioning services for groups with specific needs simply because public agencies and partners are unaware of those needs.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Partners will also find it more difficult to optimise their resources for more targeted outreach or service delivery.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Complete data is needed for more informed planning and decisions.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And this is why the Bill builds in oversight of each data sharing arrangement.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The Bill restricts sharing to public sector objectives under the PSGA and provides for criminal offences to ensure that external partners take their duty to protect the information seriously.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The concerns raised – about purpose, authorisation, partner readiness, accountability and incident response – are precisely the questions we must ask when we expand data sharing.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This Bill enables public agencies to better use data to serve Singaporeans and this goes to the heart of the public sector's core mandate, which Ms Tan has noted, has made real and meaningful differences to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: When more people rely on a bridge, we do not slow down progress.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: We build and we strengthen the foundations, we tighten the controls and we inspect the bridges more rigorously.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: That is the approach we are taking, with this Bill.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: This is how we serve more Singaporeans while safeguarding trust.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Progress that lasts is progress that is built on trust.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Keeping data safe is an ongoing and shared responsibility.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: We are committed to this responsibility, as we strive to serve all Singaporeans better.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: I do not see why it would be very difficult to do it.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: It will certainly not be operationally difficult to, because it is just publicising the type of data that is going to be shared.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: As well, I think, the five-year review period – I do not see why not.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: So, in the same explanation in the speech, I went on to say that there are also contractual Terms of Use that public agencies must impose on external partners for the receiving and use of all data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: Those Terms of Use will hold our external partners liable, should they misuse the data.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: The reason why I said that the Member may have misunderstood was that the point raised earlier was about whether our citizens will benefit from the data sharing.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: I needed to clarify that the PSGA only allows for data sharing for Public Service objectives.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: There is no sharing for commercial gains and therefore, there is no need for citizens to check whether or not private companies or organisations are gaining from this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for Minister of State Lau?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: And second of all, could the Minister of State respond on my five-year review period point, please.

speaker: Ms Jasmin Lau
text: And I think on the second question, we have said that we will review what is feasible as we gain more experience with this Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for Minister of State Lau?
